Century of Disunity

The First Hochdeutsch Empire established immediately after the coronation of the first Hochkaiser in Dresden would last for three centuries. In the final years of the First Empire from 413 to 501 after coronation, also known as the Late Imperial Period, the Empire would begin to fragment. Imperial authority from the throne in Dresden had begun a long erosion since the Hochkaisers capitulation to feudal lords in 407. The Fourth Ettlingen War, based on a struggle between the crown and local authority had resulted in a resounding defeat for loyalist forces. At the siege of Büdingen, the loyalist forces surrendered after eight months of siege allowing the feudal lords to capture the Hochkaiser. Under threat of his life, the feudal lords would force the Hochkaiser to sign the Büdingen Documents which would greatly reduce the scope of his power. Rule of law, lowered taxes and other important aspects would be set as precedent through this document. During the beginning of the Late Imperial Period fragmentation would continue as local lords and the Kriegskult began to hold more and more power. However, fragmentation of centralized power would create significant issues for the Hochdeutsch. The decline of the standing imperial army and reduced investment in cavalry put the region in a significant disadvantage. By 490 AC various nomadic tribes had swept through the southern regions of the Empire, even establishing various petty kingdoms after unseating various Hochdeutsche lords. After the defeat of several northern Hochdeutsche lords against the northern nomadic groups, the First Empire would completely shatter. 

The Second Hochdeutsche Empire would be proclaimed in inland Elseyr. While it held the titles of its predecessor it wouldnt come close in scope and scale. It was strung together by a couple petty lords, led by a boy king controlled by regents and was completely cut off from oceanic trade. The emerging manor feudal system, created by the lack of regional trade, would further cement power in the hands of the lords and clergy. Serfs would act as free labor on the large tracts of land owned by the lords and the Kreigskult while the lords acted as de facto kings by imposing whatever laws they wished. Dresden had been destroyed in the struggle with the northern nomadic groups, burned to the ground in 500 with its valuables either looted or destroyed. The Hochkaiser during this period would be only a symbolic figurehead, often holed up in the imperial palace at Selmyra. While the lords held de facto control they would continue to bankroll the existence of the Hochkaiser and the imperial lineage. His existence allowed the lords to claim authority as servants of the crown as set forth in the holy texts of the Kriegskult. During this time the Hochkaiser only served as a justification for power, not an actual exercise of it. By 517 AC, one could see how the Second Hochdeutsche Empire could not live up to the legacy of the First Empire. Constant nomadic raids had nearly brought the lineage to its death knell before reunification. 

By 572 a new threat had appeared on the horizon. Muslim caliphates had begun to push from the south into the southern Hochdeutsche reaches. For a weakened Second Empire this would be the make or break moment, to defend its legacy or be annexed into a growing Emirate. When summer had arrived, the feudal armies started to mobilize but the Hochkaiser soon realized that this would not be enough. A seasonal army wouldnt be able to fight the constant onslaught of the professionally trained and equipped forces of the Caliphate. The feudal lords by themselves completely lacked the ability to field constant standing armies but the Hochkaiser could. Using appropriation of assets from the Kriegskult, the Hochkaiser Sachsen was able to raise a standing army to face the Caliphate, just in time for their first incursions. In the summer of 574, the first muslim army was spotted marching on Osterwieck. The Hochkaisers army would march south to meet them. Camping in the town, the men would rest while their attackers moved through the treacherous terrain and summer showers. Osterwiecks geography would benefit them as well. The town was built on an island between two rivers forcing the attacking army to cross them before assailing the defenders. During the crossing the Hochkaisers forces would wait before pushing the attackers back into the waters and drowning them. Around 17,000 Caliphate forces would be killed or wounded during the battle which would come to be known as the Verdict of Osterwiecks. 

First Crusade

The threat of the Caliphate soon became a catalyst for what would be known as the Selmyran Revival, a new centralization of power under the Kriegskult and the Hochkaiser. During this time the Büdingen Documents would be reversed, placing much of the former First Hochdeutsche Empire under the control of the central government. Increasingly this would be justified by the threat the Caliphate posed. 

Scholars would note this period as the beginning of the current martial culture that permeates the Kaiserreich in the modern day. The standing army created through taxes on feudal lords would almost double. Within the Hochdeutsche Empire, non-Hochdeutsche peoples would be purged by both mobs and the Hochkaisers forces. Non-Kreigskult and Christian religious texts would be removed while thousands of people in the southern reaches of the empire would be driven out. Those who didnt convert to the two accepted faiths would either be executed, sent to do hard labor in the iron mines or sold to slavers by the government for revenue. 

In 612 the Hochkaiser would call for the first of a series of Crusades against the Muslims of southern Elseyr. Along with the professional army they would also call up feudal levies in their aim to conquer the south. They would raise an army 40,000 strong and march south beginning in the summer season of 615. Unlike its successors it would see massive success due to a variety of factors. Muslim influences in the south had drastically reduced since the 500s as increasingly draconian leaders led to revolts by the Hochdeutsche and Christian populations. At the same time the force caught the Caliphate off guard as they marched south with the element of surprise. After defeating a far smaller force quickly called up by levies, the Hochdeutsche force occupied the northern part of the caliphate establishing the Hochdeutsche controlled Christian Princely States. The Principality of Schneeburg, Altenburg and Greiz would be the first to be created, meant to be a buffer between the Second Empire and the Caliphate to the south. As they went further south they would continue a string of massacres. They would burn down Kzrak after looting the old city center, destroying centuries of history and knowledge. The streets would run red with the blood of the populace as the Hochdeutsche forces broke rank to commit heinous massacres. Surrendering Caliphate soldiers would be executed as the Hochdeutsche lit fire to the fort overlooking the Kzraki harbor. By the end of their second year journey and after the destruction of several other cities they would pull back and disband. Their supplies had run out and the majority of the feudal army had to return to tend to their fields for the next harvest. 

Second and Third Crusade

The Principality of Greiz would fall in a Caliphate counteroffensive. The significant distance between Neudresden and the Princely states would deteriorate the ability to react and receive information as well as move troops. Reinforcements for the Greizians would never arrive. While the other Princely states would attempt to repel the Caliphate at Greiz they would be forced back to defend their own lands. 

Hochkaiser Sachsen IV and the lords would rally to fight the Caliphate. However, the drowning of the Hochkaiser near a lake at the imperial palace at Selmyra would force them to delay their attack. Three years later when they arrived they found staunch Caliphate resistance at Greiz forcing them back. A series of failed sieges, where they were driven back by the Islamic reinforcements would push them further and further out of the south until only two Princely states were left. During this time a small contingent of Caliphate cavalry would ride to Selmyra and burn down the palace, only lightly defended due to the Guard Korps being pulled to the crusade. The lords would return to Selmyra defeated in the winter of 672. 

The Third Crusade would be mounted in a defensive response to the movement of Caliphate forces into the southern Kaiserreich. At the Battle of Büdingen the Hochkaiser would be defeated and force a withdrawal to Selmyra. The limited forces at Selmyra would push the Hochkaiser to withdraw to Dresden as Selmyra was burned to the ground by the Caliphate forces. Eventually the enemy would withdraw without claiming significant territory but by now the Hochdeutsche Empire had been cowed. 

Fourth Crusade

The Fourth Crusade would involve the massing of a large Hochdeutsche army in 699 to invade the southern states once again. After incorporating several northern tribes into his territories, Hochkaiser Wilhelm V turned his gaze once again onto the Caliphate. The Caliphate in recent years had broken down into constant civil war between regional governors which controlled various emirates. Tax farmers as well, holding outsized power, would also field armies to protect their interests. Into this chaotic situation the Hochkaiser struck the weakened Caliphate, quickly resizing Greiz and moving south to claim further territory. 

Moving south they would claim Jannah and other towns surrounding the Princely states, further expanding their buffer. However, in the winter of 700 their assault would stall. Scorched earth strategies by a newly appointed Caliph had reduced the readily available supplies that the Hochdeutsche forces used to move quickly. Wells were poisoned, fields were burned and sympathetic Hochdeutsche minorities were slaughtered. In response they would begin to commit mass atrocities against the peoples of the south, burning down major cities and looting wealth as they went. In the end the Fourth Crusade would prove largely successful, pulling large swathes of the northern Caliphate into the Hochdeutsche Empire. 

In the aftermath of the Fourth Crusade large amounts of non-Hochdeutsche people would be expelled from the newly established Princely states, rapidly reversing the Caliphates influence. Influx of refugees would be sent to the Caliphate causing a plague to spread rapidly in the south and across the world as the Calphates trading vessels moved across the world. As the plaque moved through the Hochdeutsche Empire it would have unprecedented effects. Almost a quarter of the population, largely urban, would die due to the plague. The significant reduction of the serf population would reduce the power of the feudal lords. Lacking significant stocks of cheap labor they would cede more power to the populace and the Hochkaiser. 

The plague would also have a freezing effect on the wars between the Hochdeutsche Empire and the southern Islamic emirates. Reductions in the feudal levies on both sides would significantly weaken eachothers fighting forces, making a large scale war now infeasible. During this time, large swathes of the royal Hochkaiser family would die off. Between 709 and 739 the Hochdeutsche Empire would have ten different monarchs, ascending usually due to the their predecessors overthrow or death of plague. To explain the plague, the Kriegskult determined that the plague was a result of the Ersten Kaisers wrath for housing non-Hochdeutsche peoples within the Empire. Mobs of peasants would roam the Empire killing off those not part of the majority ethnic group. The plague would also be blamed on the southern emirates with the widespread destruction of the remnants of Caliphate culture in the Hochdeutsche Empire. Their texts would be burned, foreigners would be executed on sight and trade with the southern states would be completely prohibited. 

Fifth Cruasde

The Fifth Crusade would become infamous for being one of the largest Kriegskult defeats to the Caliphate. During this time the Caliphate had reformed and reunited after the plague, with the Hochkaiser calling for another crusade to restore Hochdeutsche influence. This would begin in 811 with the infamous call to crusade from the new royal palace at Neudresden. The Crusaders would pay the city states of Vaslano and Panesa to ferry them from Büdingen to the southern coastal regions of the Caliphate to strike at their heartland. When the Crusaders were unable to pay they would sack the nearby town of Sachsen which would turn out to be Hochdeutsche territory. 

For this the Kreigskult would excommunicate the Crusaders but would later absolve the non-Panesan members for their actions. In the south, a petty Kingdom would promise the Crusaders 200,000 gold marks in exchange for helping them return to power. Upon reaching the mainland they would realize that the King wouldnt be able to pay resulting in the looting of the city. This would ultimately weaken the southern Kingdoms allowing the Caliphate later to conquer them. 

Collapse of the Third Empire

A string of weak rulers would shake the foundations of the Third Hochdeutsche Empire. Hochkaiser Friedrick IV would become infamous as the one who was defeated by rebelling southern lords. A coalition of lords in 833 had broken away when the Hochkaiser raised their taxes in a campaign to increase the state's power while increasing revenue. The Eisen River Plan as it was known would tax a variety of goods exported by the lands owned by those lords, primarily the wine grown on the banks of the Eisen River basin. Once the southern lords organised to oppose those taxes, the Hochkaiser would march south with the Guard Korps. During a night march, however, a group of peasants loyal to the lords would drag the Hochkasier off his horse and stab him multiple times. Days later Friedrick would die from the infection of his wounds while the perpetrators were hanged publicly. 

The death of Hochkaiser Friedrick IV would lead to a succession crisis. With no direct heir once having died at the age of 19, there were a couple contenders. His younger brother and the powerful northern lords backing him including Baron Heinrich of Sachsen contended he was the closest to the lineage. However, the southern lords would champion a cousin of the late Hochkasier, who they believed would support greater autonomy. In the south, the feudal lord would call up their levies while Baron Heinrich attempted to pull together the remnants of the great Hochdeutsche standing army. The southern feudal armies would be on the march by July of 835 while the Baron had pulled together a rag tag group of the former hawkish inner circle. 

Upon seeing the massive feudal army arrayed before him, the Baron would take the younger brother and flee the city of Neudresden. Once the feudal army arrived at Neudresden they would completely sack the city. The glory of the Second Imperial Era would come to a close as it burned. Homes and businesses would be destroyed en masse while the Hochkaisers palace, now sitting abandoned would be looted with great swathes of it destroyed. Later, during the movement of this loot south much of it would be lost as barges carrying the supplies would sink into the Eisen River. Baron Heinrich would later be captured at Bad Sachsen and forced to capitulate. Following a treaty of surrender, the Neudresden Treaty, the feudal lords would gain much more power pushing the region back again into an era of disunity. 

The younger brother, declared a pretender by the southern lords, would be executed by the feudal soldiers while being transported to the south for his imprisonment. According to speculation Baron Karl I had ordered his men to discreetly drown the man as they moved past the Selmyran lakes. All they had to do was allow him to wear his armor before pushing him over the side of the boat as they rowed across the surface. Baron Heinrich would suffer a much worse fate as the main backer of the revolt. Upon being brought to Schwarzburg castle he would be tortured for information on his fellow conspirators before being hanged by the order of Baron Karl I. 

The Kriegskult had also played a critical role in the coup. While the stated purpose of the Kriegskult was to augment the Hochkaiser the leadership had quickly started to play a large role in politics. In return for their support the southern Barons had promised that they would establish the Kriegskult Staats in the northern Hochdeutsche Empire, a region where the Kriegskult would be fully in control. Using this they would seat the cousin of the Hochkaiser as the Emperor with the full blessing of the Kriegskult. 

In 837, Hochkaiser Wenzel I would be crowned as the new Hochkaiser by the side of the southern lords who had appointed him. While the coronation would be grand with various exotic beasts and products brought from across Erene to celebrate the event, the truth was that the Hochkaiser had been completely gutted. The old empire now was dead along with the previous Hochkaiser, drowned by the Barons. The Neudresden Treaty had locked in multiple changes to the governmental system. Now the Hochkasier had been completely removed of his ability to raise taxes or any sort of charge. In addition to this the northern territories had  been carved up into various petty kingdoms controlled by the south while the Kreigskult Staats were established as well. The southern states were given de facto autonomy with no standing army in their way. 

While the Barons would profit greatly from the removal of taxes and checks on their power the Hochdeutsche Empire as a whole would languish. Decades later in 890 the majority of the former Empires infrastructure had completely collapsed or worn down. Great aqueducts which moved water to city centers had fallen apart and gone into disrepair. The Kaiser Ways, roads which connected the Hochdeutsche Empire had worn away or were undefended from bandits. In the south the victors had become increasingly isolated from the north, readopting the manor system they had relied on and bringing back slavery. The most important development however was the destruction of the standing army. Major incursions by the Caliphates would no longer be defended from with only significantly weaker feudal levies standing in their way. By 900 the Islamic emirates had advanced almost to Neudresden before being pushed back by lack of supplies and a peasant revolt. 

By this time the Hochdeutsche Empire's connections with the rest of the world had broken down. Its longstanding exports of olive oil, wine and other products had completely crashed with little ships being produced now in the southern regions of Panesa and Valsondara. Production of excess goods began to grind to halt by the fall of Neudresden with major manufacturers being destroyed. The south would face long term economic decline as well as its valuable wine and oil trades began to fall apart. 

The Four Barons

While the region declined the brutal violence would not. Bandits now roamed free on the roads, able to freely attack the populace without any retaliation. Many peasants outright stopped traveling and remained in their town, the few who did were often robbed and killed as they attempted to ride to the cities. The cities themselves were thrown into chaos as the trade and infrastructure they relied upon began to fall apart. Lack of government funds would pummel critical infrastructure in cities including the plumbing and aqueducts as disease became more and more widespread decimating urban centers. 

The destruction of the major cities of Neudresden, Selmyra, Eisenstadt and Büdingen or their decline would mark a regression back to rural living. In this time various Barons would wage war against each other to attempt to consolidate their own power. While they were able to field armies far smaller than the Hochdeutsche Empire they were able to still commit immense atrocities. Baron Ludwig II in his raids against his rivals in the north would become infamous for executing entire villages before he was assassinated in his sleep. Oftentimes to quell potential revolts from the brutally oppressed serf populace the Barons would publicly execute those who they found to be subversive to their interests. Knights, now unemployed due to the collapse of the Hochdeutsche standing army, would become mercenaries servicing the Barons. 

Over time four different distinct houses would consolidate the most power. The Haus von Hohenkrone, located in the central plains, would have the closest ties to the old Hochkaiser led government. Led by a descendant of the Hochkaiser they would support the reestablishment of a Fourth Hochdeutsche Empire but would be unable to do so. Their possession of the core cities of Selmyra and Büdingen, although decayed, made them powerful. By 917, the dawn of the Four Baron War, they would be led by Baron Gottfried III of Selmyra, who at the time was seven. His regent, Countess Gottfried, his mother, would hold the majority of power throughout this time. 

Baron Karl V, the descendant of Baron Karl I, was the patriarch of Haus von Eisenwald. His vast holdings of the agriculturally productive southern Eisen River regions and deep connections with the Kreigskult and the Kriegskult Staats would make him exceptionally powerful. Among the four it was estimated that Haus Eisenwald would be able to call up the most feudal levies in the possibility of war making them extremely powerful. Even as trade declined they would keep their hold on the remaining productive ports in the south which connected to North Vespuria. Their virtual monopoly on the limited trade and ability to contract mercenaries would also add to their power projection. 

Baron Hrodgar III of Haus von Sturmfels controlled the majority of the far northern reaches of the decaying Third Hochdeutsche Empire. A descendant of the nomadic peoples that Hochkaiser Sachsen I had conquered, he and his people had pledged fealty to the Hochkaiser. Their longstanding alliance with the Haus von Hohenkrone posed formidable as well as their vast northern territory being hard to assail or hold for long periods of time by foreign forces. The north would also hold vast gold deposits that the other Hauses would lack, allowing them to hold significant financial power. 

Baron Klemens XI of Haus von Greiz controlled the former Princely states that held the line against the Caliphate. While he lacked the massive resources available to the others he was able to hold massive armies due to the constant threat posed by the Caliphate from the south. For the same reason many of the houses were hesitant to attack the Greiz for fear of escalating and causing a Caliphate attack with the Greizians removed. 

The First Four Baron War

Tension between the four Barons would be high and the flame would be lit in 920. The death of Baron Hrodgar while on the hunt in his woods would trigger a succession crisis in the northern territories. Haus von Hohenkrone would back his younger brother while Haus von Eisenwald would march north to plant themselves in power. Haus von Hohenkrone would take a detachment south to Osterwieck to stop their crossing of the river. After heavy bombardment, however, Haus von Hohenkrone was forced to pull back from Osterwieck and would abandon the town as they headed north. Osterwieck would be one of the few towns that would come out of the conflict unscathed, with Baron Karl IV restraining his troops and enforcing heavy discipline. 

As the Haus von Hohenkrone pulled back to the Eisenstadt mountain gap, Baron Karl IV would continue to pursue them relentlessly. During the battle, the movement of troops through the narrow gap would be a mistake with various nomadic allies of Haus von Hohenkrone pushing down projectiles onto the incoming army. After days of this pursuit the Baron and half of his army would make it through the Eisenstadt gap. Although he took heavy losses, he had made it to the northern half of the Empire and still with more troops than the others. On the field outside of Selmyra, the opposing armies of the north and south would face each other. The Barons, hoping to avoid further casualties, would negotiate a settlement to the conflict. Baron Gottfried would be married to the daughter of Baron Karl IV forming the Haus von Hohenkrone und Eisenwald which still exists today. 

Once the deal was sealed Baron Karl IV would return home but would drown in the Eisen River on his way back. 

Fourth Hochdeutsche Empire

The Fourth Hochdeutsche Empire would be proclaimed by the Hause von Hohenkrone und Eisenwald in 1011. Hochkaiser Theobald II of Neudresden would be the first crowned Hochkaiser of the Fourth Empire. This period of power, known as the Neudresden Revival or the New Imperial Era would mark a significant expansion of the Empire. The standing army would be recreated and reformed to become one of the best fighting forces in Elseyr. A quick war in 1015 would take out the remaining Caliphate and refold them into the Hochdeutsche realm. Infrastructure would be rebuilt and funds would be placed into education and the military. The new imperial palace would be one of the largest in Hochdeutsche history, being built in the capital of Neudresden. The dome itself was so large that it would hold its own atmosphere. During this period the Kreigskult Staats, Princely States and the Caliphate would be folded into the Empire. 

Neudresden 1963

The University of Büdingen in January had discovered what the Central Military Commission believed to be one of the most important discoveries for military application. The men at the Büdingen University Atomic Research Institute had discovered how to split the atom. In the Central Military Building in 1963 in Neudresden the top scientists and generals of the era would gather. For hours they weighed how to acquire the fissile material required to construct a nuclear weapon. Southern deposits they had discovered had large amounts of uranium, a material necessary for the development of nuclear weapons. 

Mining would begin in 1965 with large amounts of uranium being extracted and stored by the Reichswehr. The extraction of uranium would be limited to only state owned enterprises controlled by the Reichswehr. In 1967 enough uranium for a prototype atomic bomb would be established. By 1969 the Reichswehr would test the Büdingen-4 model underground at the Saxonia Nuclear Facility. After proving successful the Reichswehr would begin the production of nuclear weapons.

In last ditch evasive maneuvers the fighter jets would begin to break up, supposedly to prevent target clumping. However, the Hydronians hadnt realized the AAMs werent proximity fused but rather meant to directly hit each individual aircraft. 

Steady datalink connections along with onboard weak frequency, constantly hopping radar would hunt down each aircraft individually, their evasive maneuvers having little impact on the operation. With those countermeasures it would be unlikely that the four squadrons would be able to make it out of the air alive. Whether they were clumped together or not wouldnt matter, the missiles were tracking the individual aircraft for air-to-air kills. 

The SM-6 anti-air missiles aboard the CSGs guided missile cruisers would hunt down the enemy aircraft as well. These missiles which reached speeds over mach 4 would be extremely hard to intercept. 

Although the Kaiserreich had destroyed the majority of the Hydronian anti-air, a select batch of Hydronian anti-air had been activated, launching missiles towards the Reichswehr jets. However, the long-range distance maintained by the J-15Es gives the fleet plenty of time to intercept the incoming anti-air missiles using their KKVs. The majority of missiles are shot down before reaching the aircraft but one jet is shot down with the pilot successfully ejecting and later being picked up by helicopter. 

The rest of the jets would exploit the activation of the air defenses. Hydronian anti-air had exposed its locations once again with activation and now the rest of the jets moved to counterattack. The REG-3000 anti-radiation missiles would be used once again. The missiles, locking onto even momentary activation of radar would home in on their locations. Its small cross section and small payload would allow it to move extremely quickly to avoid interception as well as its cross section being nearly undetectable to radar. Its ability to go faster than mach 2 would allow it to avoid most interception systems.
